title: Sleep, and the bird on a string
hookLine: the mind flies everywhere, then lands where it is tied
carry: that you are: your deepest self is Being
tomorrow: a group project, one grade. whose work is whose, once it's done?

cards: Midnight. One app, then another, then a third, and nothing lands. Then, mid-scroll, the phone slides out of your hand and you're gone.
The Chandogya has a picture for nights like that. A bird tied to a post by a string. It flies off this way, then that way, finds nowhere else to land, and settles right where it's tied.

teach.b: Learn from me about sleep, the father says. When a person sleeps, he has merged with Being. He has gone to his own.
He hears it inside the word for sleeping, svapiti: sva, one's own, and apita, gone into. So in this teaching, falling asleep is a nightly homecoming. Then the bird.

teach.h: THE BIRD SETTLES WHERE IT'S TIED.
teach.b: It flies in every direction, finds no resting place anywhere else, and settles where it's bound. The mind, he says, is the same.

teach.h: THE MIND IS BOUND TO THE BREATH.
teach.b: It flies everywhere, finds no rest, and settles in the breath, because the mind is bound to the breath. And at the end of this teaching, the father says it.
That which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self. That is the real. That is the self.
That you are, Shvetaketu. This is the teaching of the atman, said plainly: under the flying mind and the sleeping body is a self that was never apart from Being. Notice where it lands.
Not in a temple, not on a mountaintop. In a talk about sleep, said to one son, by name. And Shvetaketu doesn't say he's got it.
He says: please, sir, teach me more. So be it, my dear, says his father.

how: In Vedanta study, Chandogya 6.8 is read as the place where the refrain tat tvam asi begins, and a teacher may start with its pictures of sleep and of the bird on a string.

o: that is yours: you own the whole world
that is far from you, so go and seek it
that you are: you are the finest essence

games.q: sleep, the bird, the breath. tap the pairs.

s: tat tvam asi is first spoken in a grand scene at a temple
it comes at the end of a talk about sleep, said by a father to his son, by name.
the father hears the word for sleeping as 'gone into one's own'
svapiti: sva, one's own, and apita, gone into. sleep is a homecoming.

games.q: at rest time, a camper is scared to fall asleep: 'where do i go?' which picture does the Chandogya offer?
o: sleep is going home: the sleeper has gone to his own.
sleep is a blank gap where nothing at all is there.
sleep is a trip far away from who you really are.
games.why: the father hears svapiti as sva, one's own, and apita, gone into. the sleeper has merged with Being: gone home, not gone missing.

practice: Let the body settle the way a bird lands: shoulders down, hands open in your lap, weight sinking into the seat. When the mind flies off, let it fly until it tires, then let it come down on the breath, the post it's tied to.
Land as often as it takes.

wordCard.voice: Tat tvam asi: that you are. Here the father says it, right after the sleeper gone home and the bird that settles where it's tied.

orig.note: Sanskrit: he sleeps. The father hears it as sva apita, gone into one's own.

carryVoice: Carry this: that you are, and your deepest self is Being, the post the bird comes home to. Rest well tonight.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.1–2 (when a person sleeps he has merged with Being, gone to his own, so they say svapiti; as a bird tied by a string flies in every direction and, finding no rest elsewhere, settles where it is bound, so the mind settles in the breath, for the mind is bound to the breath)

Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (that which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self; that is the real; that is the self; that you are, Shvetaketu; please, sir, teach me more; so be it, my dear)
